title: Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of building, releasing, and maintaining an api in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to preparing a production configuration.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers building, releasing, and maintaining an api within practical application development. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use building, releasing, and maintaining an api to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is predictable client-server contracts, resource naming, typed parameters and correct HTTP semantics.

content_blocks.title: Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API: concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step flow for Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API: Preparing a production configuration, Setting up automated testing, Running migrations safely, Deploying to a hosting service
content_blocks.caption: Visual-first overview before the worked example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API matters because it is part of practical application development. In practice, focus on predictable client-server contracts, resource naming, typed parameters and correct HTTP semantics. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: Preparing a production configuration
items.text: For preparing a production configuration, collect measurable evidence from a local or staging environment. Keep configuration environment-specific, avoid logging secrets, establish a rollback path, and do not claim performance or availability without measurements.

items.title: Setting up automated testing
items.text: Use setting up automated testing to make behavior observable and repeatable. Specify one normal case, one invalid or missing-input case, and the expected status or diagnostic. A passing happy path alone is not enough evidence.

items.title: Running migrations safely
items.text: Apply running migrations safely against a disposable database and synthetic data first. Make transaction ownership and cleanup explicit, parameterize values, and verify constraints and behavior after failures before considering a deployment.

items.title: Deploying to a hosting service
items.text: For deploying to a hosting service, collect measurable evidence from a local or staging environment. Keep configuration environment-specific, avoid logging secrets, establish a rollback path, and do not claim performance or availability without measurements.

items.title: Monitoring the running application
items.text: For monitoring the running application, collect measurable evidence from a local or staging environment. Keep configuration environment-specific, avoid logging secrets, establish a rollback path, and do not claim performance or availability without measurements.

items.title: Planning updates and recovery
items.text: Use planning updates and recovery as a design decision rather than a keyword to memorize. State the input and expected result, identify the boundary conditions, and connect the concept to the surrounding FastAPI request lifecycle.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API
content_blocks.code:
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.ready = True
    yield
    app.state.ready = False

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
content_blocks.expected_output: The lifespan setup runs before requests are served and cleanup runs at shutdown.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run locally and watch startup/shutdown logs; do not use this example to store secrets in code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.

Run it only in a local virtual environment or a separately isolated runner with resource/time/network limits. Security examples are sketches, not complete production authentication or authorization systems.

task: Create a small reviewable artifact for “Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API”: explain its goal, cover the listed subtopics, show an example with expected result, then include one edge case and how you would verify it.
hints: Start with “Preparing a production configuration” and state the required inputs, output and assumptions.
Change one thing at a time; check the official reference and capture the actual response/error instead of guessing.
Include a negative/edge-case check and document which behavior remains untested.
expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.

summary: Building, Releasing, and Maintaining an API belongs to the broader goal of predictable client-server contracts, resource naming, typed parameters and correct HTTP semantics.
Use the source subtopics as the completeness checklist and verify expected results rather than relying on intuition.
Examples in this course are illustrative until technically reviewed and executed on a supported local environment.
